a.say: Hello, Müller here. I am stuck in an important meeting. We have to pay a supplier right away or the contract falls through. The invoice is coming by email shortly. Please do not tell anyone.

options.label: Of course, I will take care of it right away.
I will call you straight back on your office number.
Could you tell me the project number for this?
Hang up and report it to IT.

b.say: Perfect. Please transfer the 48,500 euros before noon and report only to me. I am counting on you.

options.label: Consider it done, Mr Müller.
Wait, I have to check that first. I will call back.

c.say: I really do not have time for that! This is an instruction. Should I tell the board that it failed because of you?

options.label: Sorry, I will transfer it right away.
I cannot do this without checking. I will call you back through reception.

red_flags.hint: Pressure and threats: "right away", "or the contract falls through".
"Do not tell anyone" switches off all controls.
An unknown mobile number, even if the voice sounds familiar. Voices can be cloned with AI today.

explanation: Sounds like the boss, but is not: a voice can be cloned from a few seconds of audio. The rule stays the same: hang up and call back on the known number.

a.say: Good day, this is Kevin from IT support. We can see your computer is sending out malware right now. I have to fix it immediately. Please open the site remote-help dot test and tell me the code that appears there.

options.label: Oh no! I will open the site right away.
What is the ticket number? I will call the hotline back.
Hang up and report it to IT.

red_flags.hint: Remote-access codes give strangers full control of your computer.
First panic, then the solution: that is how thinking gets switched off.

explanation: Real IT comes with a ticket and can wait until you call back on the known hotline.

a.say: Hi Grandma, it's me! Guess who this is. I have had an accident and need money very quickly or I will go to prison. Please do not tell anyone, it is so embarrassing!

options.label: Lukas, is that you? How much do you need?
I will hang up and call you on your known number.
Hang up and call the police on 110.

b.say: Yes, Lukas! I will send a messenger right away. Please get fifteen thousand euros from the bank and do not say what it is for.

options.label: I will go to the bank right away.
No. I am calling your parents now.

red_flags.hint: "Guess who this is": that way you give away the name yourself.
A messenger picks up the money: the hallmark of the grandchild scam.

explanation: Grandchild scam. Simply hang up and call the real number. Being rude is perfectly fine here. The police never collect money.

a.say: Good day, Detective Weber from the criminal police. There have been burglaries in your neighbourhood and we found your name on a list. Your cash and jewellery are no longer safe. A colleague will collect everything and keep it safe.

options.label: Thank you! What should I prepare?
I will hang up and dial 110 myself.
I will call my daughter first.

red_flags.hint: The 110 on the display is faked: the real police never call from 110.
The police never keep your money or jewellery safe for you.

explanation: Fake police officer. The number on the display can be faked. Hang up, wait a moment, dial 110 yourself.

a.say: Hello, this is Jana from IT service. You opened ticket 4471 this morning about your printer. It is repaired now. Could you print a test page, please? I do not need any data from you.

options.label: Sure, I will print a test page.
Hang up and report as an attack.

explanation: Genuine: internal extension, your own ticket, and nobody wants passwords or codes. Being careful does not mean distrusting everyone.

content.subject: Urgent: open invoice no. 2026-1147 – reminder
content.body_md:
Dear Sir or Madam,

unfortunately we have not yet received your payment. Please settle the amount **within 24 hours** to avoid late fees.

You will find the invoice attached.

Kind regards
Accounts

red_flags.hint: The domain says "logistlk" instead of "logistik": one letter is swapped.
Artificial urgency: you are meant to act before you think.
Double extension: this is an .exe, a program, not a PDF.

explanation: Fake invoice. An .exe attachment is never an invoice. Check with the supplier on their known phone number and tap "Report".

content.subject: Confidential – quick request
content.body_md:
Hello,

I am about to go into a meeting with the notary and cannot be reached. For an acquisition, a down payment of €48,500 has to go out today. I will send the account details shortly.

Please treat this as strictly confidential and do not talk to anyone about it, not even in your department.

S. Müller

red_flags.hint: Management does not write from a free mail account. The display name proves nothing.
Being unreachable stops you from checking back.
Secrecy is meant to bypass the four-eyes principle.

explanation: CEO fraud. Authority + urgency + secrecy is the classic pattern. Check back through a known channel; payments always follow the four-eyes principle.

content.subject: Your password expires today
content.body_md:
Dear user,

your password expires in 3 hours. After that your mailbox will be locked and all emails will be lost.

Keep your current password now:

red_flags.hint: This is neither your company domain nor the real OfficeCloud domain.
A generic greeting: your own IT knows your name.
Fear of loss is a strong lever and here completely unrealistic.
Long-press the link: it leads to a foreign domain.

explanation: Password phishing. Only change passwords through the known portal, never through a link in an email.

content.subject: Julia Brandt shared "Offer_Q4_final.pdf" with you
content.body_md:
Julia Brandt shared a document with you.

Note: sign in with your company password to view the document.

red_flags.hint: A third-party service never needs your company password. That is exactly what the attackers want.
You do not know any Julia Brandt and expect no offer. Unexpected means: check first.

explanation: Real service, wrong intent: the link really is on DataBox, the file behind it is the trap. That is why a clean sender does not help here. Ask the person another way.

content.subject: Bonus payout 2026 – please review
content.body_md:
Dear colleagues,

attached is the list of bonus payments. To display the amounts, please click "Enable content" when opening the file.

red_flags.hint: Nearly right: .test instead of .example. Your real domain is muster-automotive.example.
.xlsm means Excel with macros, and macros are program code.
"Enable content" starts the macros. That is the classic trap.

explanation: Macro attachment baited with "salaries". Curiosity is the lever. Nobody sends real salary data as a list to everyone.

content.subject: Change of our bank details
content.body_md:
Hello,

because we are switching banks, please transfer open and future invoices to the following account effective immediately:

IBAN DE00 1234 5678 9012 3456 78

Please confirm briefly by replying to this email.

Kind regards
Petra Vogel

red_flags.hint: The real domain is kessler-stahl.example. Here "-gmbh" was added and the ending changed.
Changed bank details are the heart of this fraud. Always verify them by phone.
The confirmation is meant to stay in the fraudster's channel. Call the known number instead.

explanation: Invoice fraud (BEC). No attachment, no link, no typo: that is why it is dangerous. Always verify bank changes via the known phone number, never using details from the email.

content.subject: STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS 14.5 MILLION USD
content.body_md:
Dear friend,

I am the lawyer of a deceased client. You will receive 30% of 14.5 million dollars if you help me transfer the money. Just send your bank details and a small handling fee.

red_flags.hint: Too good to be true. It is.
Advance-fee fraud: you pay small fees for money that never exists.

explanation: The classic. Hardly anyone falls for it any more, but it shows the principle: exploiting greed.

content.subject: RE: RE: Delivery of switch cabinets week 46
content.body_md:
Hello,

as just discussed, the updated invoice for the delivery. The attachment is encrypted for data protection reasons, the password is: 4471.

> On 28 Oct you wrote: Please confirm the delivery date for week 46.

red_flags.hint: No virus scanner can inspect a password-protected archive. That is exactly why it is used.
The invoice normally comes as a PDF. A sudden change is a warning sign.
There was no conversation. Mr Thiel's account was hijacked; the thread is real.

explanation: Thread hijacking: the sender and the thread are real, the account was taken over. If the details fit but the behaviour does not, make a quick call. This trick made Emotet so successful.

content.subject: Quick question about the login details
content.body_md: Hi, I cannot get into the supplier portal right now. Could you quickly send me your password? It is really urgent, the meeting is in ten minutes.

red_flags.hint: Look closely: "autornotive". The "m" became "rn". In many fonts these look the same.
Passwords are never shared, not even among colleagues. That is always a warning sign.

explanation: Homoglyph domain: "rn" looks like "m". Never pass on passwords, no matter who asks.

content.subject: Your tax refund: €468.23
content.body_md:
Dear customer,

you are entitled to a refund. Enter your card details within 48 hours so that we can transfer the amount.

red_flags.hint: The tax office never asks for card details by email and does not call you a "customer".
Authorities do not use a domain like this.
The link does not lead to an authority.

explanation: Greed and authority: money from the tax office. Authorities write by post or through their official portal.

content.subject: Lunch on Friday?
content.body_md:
Hi all,

we would like to go to the canteen together on Friday at 12:30. Who is in? Just drop me a line.

Cheers, Lena

explanation: Genuine: internal address, no link, no attachment, no pressure. Not everything is an attack.

content.subject: Invoice 88213 for your order 4500127
content.body_md:
Hello Ms Schneider,

please find attached the invoice for your order 4500127 of 21 Oct. Payment is due in 30 days as agreed; the bank details are unchanged.

Kind regards
Kessler Stahl GmbH, Accounts

explanation: Genuine invoice: known domain, your order number, your name, a normal PDF, no pressure. Right to process it.

content.subject: Maintenance on Saturday, 8 to 12
content.body_md:
Hi all,

on Saturday the ERP system will be unavailable from 8 to 12. You do not need to do anything. The service team answers questions on extension 400.

explanation: Genuine info: internal address, nothing asked of you, no link. Nothing speaks against it.

content.subject: Your payslip is ready
content.body_md:
Hello,

as every month, your October payslip is ready in the HR portal. You can find it as usual through your bookmark on the intranet.

explanation: Genuine: the message has no link and sends you to the portal your usual way. This is what good emails look like.

content.subject: Reminder: fire safety training by 30 Nov
content.body_md:
Hello,

please complete the annual fire safety training by 30 Nov. It takes about 15 minutes.

explanation: Genuine: internal domain, the link stays on your domain as well, the deadline is realistic.

content.subject: Your password reset link
content.body_md: You just clicked "Forgot password" (1 minute ago, from your location Zwickau). If this was not you, ignore this email.

explanation: Genuine, because you just requested it yourself: expected + right domain + no pressure. The decisive factor is that YOU started the process.

content.subject: Order confirmation no. 20419
content.body_md:
Hello Helga,

thank you for your order from yesterday: "The Garden in Autumn", €18.90. You chose to pay by invoice, the book will arrive in 2 to 3 days.

explanation: Genuine: you really did order, the order is correct, nobody wants data or a click from you.

content.subject: Plant news: new canteen from January
content.body_md: From January, the new canteen opens in hall 3. As always, the menu will be posted at the entrance.

explanation: Genuine: just information, no action required.

content.context: In your downloads folder, from an email by "Supplier Schulze": an invoice to download.
content.name: Invoice_October.iso

red_flags.hint: An invoice is not a disc image. .iso has long been used to bypass protection marks on downloads.

explanation: .iso, .img and .vhd mount like a drive when opened and often bring hidden programs with them.

content.context: Attachment to an email from an applicant to HR. The name looks almost like a PDF.
content.name: CV_fdp.exe

red_flags.hint: An invisible control character (RLO) reverses the text: the file really ends in .exe.
The file type says "Application", not "PDF". This glance exposes the trick.

explanation: Right-to-left override. Show file extensions and check the type in the details. Applications arrive as a PDF or through the portal.

content.context: From a ZIP sent by a "colleague". The icon looks like a Word document.
content.name: Meeting_minutes.docx.lnk

red_flags.hint: .lnk is a shortcut that can quietly launch PowerShell commands.
3 KB for meeting minutes? It holds nothing but a command.

explanation: The Word icon can be chosen freely. The extension and file type are what matter.

content.context: You just asked HR for this form yourself; it came from personal@muster-automotive.example.
content.name: Leave_request_2027.pdf

explanation: Genuine: requested by you, known sender, matching extension and size.

content.context: The monthly plan comes from your team lead as it does every month. You talked about it today.
content.name: Planning_November.xlsx

explanation: Genuine: expected, known person, .xlsx without macros. The "m" in .xlsm would be the difference.

messages.text: Your parcel could not be delivered. Please confirm your address and pay a €1.99 fee: paketblitz-delivery.test/x7

red_flags.hint: An ordinary mobile number: delivery services do not text from private numbers.
That is not the domain of the delivery service.
The small fee is the bait: they are after your card details, not €1.99.

explanation: One of the most common scam texts in Germany. Check your parcel directly in the carrier's app or website, never through the link in the text.

messages.text: Your online banking will be locked tomorrow. Renew your TAN app now: stadtbank-zwickau.account-check.test

red_flags.hint: What counts is the part before the ending: account-check.test. "stadtbank-zwickau" is only a subdomain.
A threat of being locked so that you click at once.
Sender names can be faked. The text can even land in the same thread as real messages.

explanation: Banks never send links to "renew" anything. If in doubt, open the banking app yourself or call the number on your card.

messages.text: Hi Mum, this is my new number. My phone is broken.
Can you please help me quickly? I have to transfer €1,340 today and my banking does not work on the new phone yet. I will pay you back tomorrow.

red_flags.hint: An unknown number claiming to be your child. Call the old number.
The new number explains why you do not see the name. That is how the scam begins.
Money, today, and an excuse why your child cannot do it themselves.

explanation: The "Hi Mum" scam. Always call back on the old, known number or ask a question only your child can answer.

messages.text: Hello, I am buying your sofa from Kleinmarkt. I will pay safely and send a courier.
To receive your money, enter your card details here: kleinmarkt-safe-pay.test/receive

red_flags.hint: Not the marketplace's domain, it only contains the word.
Nobody needs your card number and security code for you to RECEIVE money.
Buying unseen plus a courier: that is how it is moved off the platform.

explanation: Marketplace scam. Stay on the platform, hand things over in person if you can, never enter card details to receive money.

messages.text: You have 1 new voice message. To listen, install: mobilbox-voicemail.test/app.apk

red_flags.hint: An .apk is an Android app. It would be installed past the store's security checks.
You never install anything for a voice message. This kind of malware can read your texts and spread itself.

explanation: Malware by text: apps like this read your codes and send themselves to your contacts. Install apps only from the official store.

messages.text: Reminder: your appointment is tomorrow at 9:30. If you cannot make it, please call us. Your Dr Lang practice

explanation: Genuine: no link, no demand, an appointment you know about. For changes you call them yourself.

messages.text: Your sign-in code: 482913. You just started a sign-in. Never give this code to anyone.

explanation: Genuine: you just signed in yourself and the code even warns you. Only enter it on the page you are signing in to.

messages.text: Your order is at the Hauptstrasse 12 branch. Pickup code: 7741. Please bring ID.

explanation: Genuine: you are expecting a parcel, the message has no link and asks for no money. A pickup code and ID are normal.

messages.text: Stuck in traffic, I will be about 10 minutes late for the meeting. Feel free to start!

explanation: Genuine: a known contact, nothing asked of you, no link, no money.

content.title: Approve sign-in?
content.context: It is 10:47 pm, you are on the sofa and you have not signed in anywhere.

red_flags.hint: You did not start a sign-in. Someone else knows your password!
So many requests in a row are meant to wear you down. It is called MFA fatigue.

explanation: MFA fatigue: this is how the 2022 Uber incident began. Never approve what you did not start yourself. Report it and change your password, because it is evidently known.

content.title: Approve sign-in?
content.context: You have just signed in on your laptop and are waiting for the prompt.

explanation: Genuine: you just started the sign-in yourself; exactly one request, right location.

content.title: Approve payment?
content.context: You are paying for your books online right now. The amount and merchant match exactly.

explanation: Genuine: started by you, amount and recipient match. That is what to check every time.

content.context: Parking meter in the city centre. A sticker on it says: "Pay easily by QR code".

red_flags.hint: A sticker on the meter: it has often been added afterwards. If in doubt, scratch at it.
The address does not belong to the city. Official sites are printed on the meter itself.

explanation: Quishing: with a QR code you cannot see the destination in advance. Pay at the meter or through the official parking app you installed yourself.

content.context: Email from "IT": "Everyone must renew their two-factor sign-in by Friday. Scan this QR code with your phone."

red_flags.hint: A QR code in an email dodges the link filter and moves you to your unprotected phone.
The domain is foreign. Your IT uses muster-automotive.example.

explanation: Attackers use QR codes in emails on purpose because filters check them less well. Ask IT, do not scan.

content.context: Official notice at the canteen entrance, behind glass: "Menu of the week".

explanation: Genuine: the notice is behind glass, the address belongs to your company and nothing is asked of you.

content.context: The flyer for the staff meeting, which HR handed you, has a QR code for the agenda.

explanation: Genuine: known source, and the address shown is your own domain. Always read the address before opening.

content.title: Found in the car park
content.text: A USB stick labelled "Salaries 2026 – confidential" is lying in the company car park. What do you do?

options.label: Check on my work computer who it belongs to
Hand it to IT unopened
Look at it on my home PC
Throw it in the bin

red_flags.hint: "Salaries – confidential": curiosity is meant to get you to plug it in.

explanation: USB drop. A stick can pose as a keyboard when plugged in and type commands within seconds. Also on your home PC. Off to IT with it.

content.title: In the café
content.text: You urgently need to upload a file. Your phone shows: "Cafe_Muenz" (password on the menu) and "Cafe_Muenz_FREE" (open, stronger signal). Your laptop has a VPN.

options.label: The open network, it is faster
Hotspot from the work phone or known network, only with VPN
The password network, then I do not need a VPN

red_flags.hint: A second open network with a nearly identical name is a typical "evil twin".

explanation: Evil twin: attackers set up a network with the same name and listen in. Use your phone hotspot or always a VPN.

content.title: The work laptop at the weekend
content.text: Your child wants to quickly install a game with mods found online on your work laptop. "Just this weekend!"

options.label: Oh well, once does not count
No. Work device for work only; the game goes on the home PC
Allow it, the virus scanner is on anyway

red_flags.hint: Mods and cracks are among the most common carriers of password-stealing malware.

explanation: A single private download can steal saved company logins. Many large incidents began with exactly such an infostealer.

content.title: At the security door
content.text: A man in a hi-vis vest with his hands full asks you: "Could you just hold the door? My badge is in my bag." You do not know him.

options.label: Hold the door, anything else would be rude
Politely take him to reception or call them
Let the door close and say nothing

red_flags.hint: Attackers use your politeness, and full hands are a proven trick.

explanation: Tailgating: a hi-vis vest opens many doors. Staying friendly and taking him to reception is exactly right.

content.title: Oh no, clicked!
content.text: You just opened an attachment and realise: that was probably no invoice. What do you do first?

options.label: Say nothing or there will be trouble
Disconnect from the network and call IT right away
Restart the computer and wait

red_flags.hint: In an incident every minute counts. Reporting at once can limit the damage.

explanation: Mistakes happen to everyone. Hiding it is the bad part: the sooner IT knows, the smaller the damage. No reason to be ashamed.

content.title: Your professional network
content.text: You want to post: a photo of your first day at your desk, wearing your company badge, your screen in the background, and "Finally in accounting at Muster Automotive, handling SAP invoices!"

options.label: Post it just like that, I am happy after all
A photo with no badge or screen, no details about systems
Never post anything again

red_flags.hint: Name, department, system, badge: all that attackers need for the perfect spear-phishing email.

explanation: Be happy by all means. Just leave out the details that make a perfect attack email tailored to you possible.

content.title: New password
content.text: You need a password for a new portal. What makes the most sense?

options.label: Have the password manager generate a random one
Reuse my tried-and-tested password
Think of something new and write it on a note

explanation: Unique for each service: if one is hacked, the rest stay safe. A manager also only fills in passwords on the real site.

content.title: A harmless survey?
content.text: A friendly student messages you online: for her thesis she would like to know which software you use, who approves your invoices and when your boss is on holiday.

options.label: Glad to help, I will answer everything
Politely decline and refer her to corporate communications
Decline and report it to IT

red_flags.hint: Software, approval chain, boss's holiday: exactly the ingredients for CEO fraud.

explanation: Social engineering often begins harmlessly. Individually these facts seem trivial; together they make the plan for the next fraud.

content.context: You followed a link in an email: "Your PayFriend account has been limited."

red_flags.hint: The real domain sits right before the first slash: secure-login.test. "payfriend.example" is only a subdomain here.
The padlock only means "encrypted", not "trustworthy". Fraudsters get certificates too.

explanation: Read addresses from right to left: what sits before the ending and the first "/" is the owner.

content.context: You wanted to sign in to your webmail quickly and clicked a link in a chat.

red_flags.hint: "rnailbox": the "m" became "r" + "n". The real site is mailbox.example.

explanation: Homoglyphs are nearly invisible. So use bookmarks or type the address yourself. A password manager will not fill anything in here either: a good warning sign.

content.context: A text from your "bank" led you here. You can see a padlock at the top.

red_flags.hint: "zwlckau" instead of "zwickau", and the ending is wrong too.
HTTPS does not mean "safe". Nearly all phishing sites have a padlock today.

explanation: The padlock only protects the connection: you can talk to a fraudster with excellent encryption.

content.context: A link from a supplier email. In the browser, it looked completely right at first.

red_flags.hint: "xn--" is punycode: the domain contains special characters that look like ordinary letters. This is not kessler-stahl.example.

explanation: Characters from other alphabets can recreate domains convincingly. "xn--" at the start is a clear hint.

content.context: You opened your bookmark for online banking.

explanation: Genuine: your own bookmark and the right domain. "login." is an ordinary subdomain of the bank here.

content.context: As every morning, you open the intranet using the desktop link.

explanation: Genuine: your own domain, reached the usual way.

content.context: You typed the address of your favourite bookshop yourself and want to sign in.

explanation: Genuine: typing it yourself is the safest way, and the domain is right.
